target: AG1’s claim that AI is broadly good for society because it improves convenience, health, productivity, accessibility, and workplace safety.
objection: AI is not good for society overall because its downsides outweigh its benefits: it can automate and deskill work, concentrate power in a few large firms, weaken critical thinking by encouraging outsourcing of reasoning, reproduce racism from biased training data, and create serious privacy risks that convenience does not offset.

target: AG2’s claim that AI is inevitably harmful and that its risks cannot be managed.
objection: AI is not inevitably harmful; it can be deployed as an assistive tool that augments people rather than replacing them, with retraining and task redesign helping workers and students shift to higher-value work instead of being displaced.

target: AG2’s claim that AI necessarily weakens students’ critical thinking.
objection: AI does not have to weaken critical thinking; it can improve it through personalized tutoring, step-by-step feedback, and exercises that require students to explain reasoning, draft work, cite sources, and revise their answers.

target: AG2’s claim that bias and racial harm make AI itself unacceptable.
objection: Bias and fairness problems are not arguments against AI in principle; they are arguments for responsible design such as audits, transparency, better data, and improved evaluation methods that can reduce biased outcomes.

target: AG2’s claim that privacy risks make AI too dangerous to use.
objection: Privacy risks can be reduced with safeguards such as access controls, data minimization, and privacy-preserving methods, so privacy concerns do not automatically make AI unacceptable.

target: AG1’s claim that risks can be managed through governance, training, audits, and safeguards.
objection: That reply assumes institutions will reliably prioritize safety over profit and will fully control AI’s real-world effects, but in practice market incentives favor scale and automation, audits and transparency often fail to catch subtle or evolving harms, education safeguards are hard to enforce, and privacy protections are undermined by AI’s ability to infer sensitive traits from limited data.

target: AG1’s claim that governance can make AI benefits dependable and risks manageable.
objection: Oversight usually lags behind deployment, accountability is diffuse across developers, vendors, and deployers, and this delay makes harms difficult to correct quickly enough to keep AI’s promised benefits dependable.

target: AG1’s claim that educational safeguards can prevent AI from undermining learning.
objection: Education safeguards are hard to enforce at scale because students and teachers under workload pressure will still use AI to generate answers, creating automation bias and allowing students to avoid truly understanding the material.

target: AG1’s claim that data minimization and access controls can adequately protect privacy.
objection: Privacy risks persist even with minimal data because AI can infer sensitive traits from behavior, text, images, and interactions, so limiting raw data does not eliminate the underlying privacy threat.

target: AG1’s claim that AI can be kept beneficial if used only in constrained, well-audited domains.
objection: Even narrow deployments will tend to expand under competitive and profit pressure into more workflows, schools, and decision points, so constrained use will not stay contained long enough to reliably prevent harms.

target: AG1’s claim that AI can broadly benefit marginalized groups through accessibility tools.
objection: AI may actually serve marginalized groups poorly in practice because it often performs badly on diverse languages, accents, dialects, and disability types, and useful tools are often paywalled or require devices, connectivity, and digital literacy that these groups may lack.

target: AG1’s claim that AI can improve accessibility and opportunity for marginalized groups.
objection: When AI is used in high-stakes settings like hiring, credit, benefits, or policing, even small bias rates can become large-scale discrimination, so the harms fall disproportionately on the same marginalized groups AI is supposed to help.

target: AG1’s claim that AI can be deployed in a narrow way without expanding surveillance.
objection: AI systems often create a data flywheel: they collect ongoing user interactions to improve performance and maintain quality, so a supposedly narrow deployment tends to expand data collection and surveillance over time.

target: AG1’s claim that audits and oversight can keep AI safe in practice.
objection: Audits are unreliable because they can be compromised by conflicts of interest, and test conditions cannot fully represent messy real-world use; as systems are updated and integrated into workflows, their capability and impact broaden faster than oversight can adapt.

target: AG1’s claim that privacy-preserving technical measures like on-device processing, federated learning, and differential privacy can make AI safe enough.
objection: Those measures do not reliably make AI socially beneficial because strong privacy-preserving architectures are expensive and often not adopted, minimized data can still reveal sensitive traits through inference, and organizations may weaken protections when they reduce performance or utility.

target: AG1’s claim that better procurement and regulation can make privacy-preserving AI the default.
objection: The theory depends on compliance that is not reliable at scale, because vendors and businesses prefer data-heavy, highly personalized systems and governance is too weak to consistently enforce safer architectures across continuously updated, opaque deployments.

target: AG1’s claim that AI’s benefits justify deployment with guardrails.
objection: AI’s benefits are often achievable with narrower, rules-based, or human-centered tools, while AI adds unique systemic risks such as black-box decision-making at scale, model monoculture, and concentration of power in a few vendors, so broad deployment is not a dependable net positive.
